- If sentiment is positive (≥0.20) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.00) and forecast is rising, cap upward momentum; model may be ignoring bearish signals.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), forecast should not immediately continue rising — introduce mean reversion bias.  
- If true outcome exceeds forecast by >5% over 3–5 days, adjust future forecasts downward by 1–2% per day to reflect momentum decay.  
- When sentiment is neutral (0.00) and forecast is flat, consider slight upward bias if recent history shows upward drift; otherwise, maintain flat.  
- If forecast is consistently below true outcome by >3% over 10+ days, increase forecast baseline by 1–2% to account for lagged market reaction.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of decline after peak), reduce forecast slope toward historical mean.
